title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We performed a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) to test whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. The design used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task the same single sampled initial model candidate was used for both arms; the baseline outcome is that single‑shot candidate’s deterministic‑validator pass/fail, and the guarded outcome is the final pass/fail after deterministic verification and ≤1 automated repair. Planned N=300 pairs; after preregistered exclusions 266 complete pairs were analysed. Baseline passes = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) passes = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Automated repair was invoked in 6 repair calls (across 300 tasks). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule the observed improvement does not reach confirmatory significance; inference is limited by very small discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0). Median repair iterations per task = 0 (preregistered H2(a) confirmed). Per‑episode end‑to‑end latency (H2(b)) was not recorded in the archived per‑episode artifacts and therefore could not be evaluated. We report the preregistered design, deterministic validation rule, recorded runtime model settings, complete numeric results, representative repair examples from the archive, contamination findings (no flagged duplicates), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and threats to validity.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being explored to translate operator intent into vendor CLI configurations and to automate NetOps workflows [1,2]. Stochastic generation can produce syntactic or semantic violations (e.g., unsafe sequencing or constraint breaches) that create operational risk; accordingly, architectures that interpose deterministic validators and bounded repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) have been proposed to improve correctness and to provide deterministic pass/fail assurance [3–5]. Prior work has proposed using Batfish‑style verification or header‑space analyses as determinising oracles inside LLM‑driven pipelines, but large‑scale, preregistered evaluations measuring the verifier‑triggered repair benefit under controlled paired designs remain limited [2,3]. We therefore asked: Does a GVR pipeline (single sampled LLM candidate + deterministic verifier + ≤1 automated repair) reduce verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures relative to the same initial candidate without repair? Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation using shared_initial_candidate semantics and deterministic validator traces that supports reproducible confirmatory inference.
sections.related_work: Work on LLM‑enabled NetOps includes intent→CLI prototypes, benchmarks (NetConfEval family), and surveys describing failure modes and grounding strategies [1,2]. Generate–verify–repair and verifier‑augmented architectures have been proposed in code generation and operational domains to reduce hallucinations and to enable deterministic validation [3,4]. Network verification tools such as Batfish and header‑space analyses have been suggested and used as oracles inside such pipelines [2,3]. Constrained‑decoding and integer‑program constrained decoding have been proposed to reduce constraint violations, but demonstrations specific to complex vendor CLIs are limited [5]. Our study differs by executing a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics with deterministic validator outputs and archived raw artifacts for auditability.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study preregistration is cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Sampling and tasks: planned N=300 independent intent pairs (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like) deterministically generated from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator; inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration. Execution contract: exactly one initial model generation per task (shared across arms); if deterministic validation failed the guarded arm could invoke at most one automated LLM repair call. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs syntactic parsing, required‑sequence checks, and reachability/constraint checks and yields a binary pass/fail primary endpoint. Model configuration: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The archived model_configuration.json records max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). An unset/null temperature value in the archived configuration is not evidence of deterministic (temperature=0) sampling; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded because no deterministic sampling seed is archived. Analysis plan: primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes; paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the primary 266‑pair analysis; preregistered sensitivity analyses for missingness treat excluded both‑arm infrastructure failures conservatively. Per the preregistration, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate: the baseline outcome is the single initial sampled candidate's deterministic‑validator pass/fail; the guarded outcome is the final pass/fail after deterministic verification and any permitted automated repair.
sections.results: Execution accounting (deterministic_reconciliation): planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 532, failed episodes = 68, complete paired units analysed = 266 (34 both‑arm provider/infra failures excluded per preregistered rules). Confirmatory primary results (n=266): baseline successes = 260/266 (0.9774436090); guarded final successes = 265/266 (0.9962406015). Paired contingency: n11=260, n10=5, n01=0, n00=1 (Table 1). Paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 → not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Provider_call_audit records stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6 (six guarded repair calls executed). Median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2(a) confirmed). Per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not recorded in per‑task archived artifacts and therefore H2(b) (median ≤ 60 s) could not be evaluated. Missingness sensitivity (treating the 34 excluded both‑arm failures as failures in a conservative N=300 analysis) yields baseline = 260/300 (0.866667), guarded = 265/300 (0.883333), paired difference = 0.016667; the discordant counts are unchanged and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Contamination checks: archived contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged exact duplicates; no items were excluded for contamination from the primary analysis.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The guarded GVR pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (≈1.88 percentage points on complete pairs). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule this improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The apparent tension between a bootstrap CI that excludes zero and an exact McNemar p > 0.05 is a known finite‑sample effect: exact two‑sided McNemar depends only on discordant counts (here n10=5, n01=0) and is discrete; resampling CIs incorporate paired sampling variability differently and may exclude zero even when the exact two‑sided p exceeds 0.05. Practical implications: for this corpus and model the baseline single‑shot pass rate is very high and repair invocations were rare (6/300), limiting headroom for the guarded repair stage to improve outcomes. Representative repair example (archived artifact): task-000008 initial shared candidate (baseline) produced a truncated/ malformed final line (“interface uplink2
”) while the guarded final output included the corrected explicit command sequence ending with “interface uplink2 admin down … interface edge1 admin up” (see archived responses for task-000008). This concrete example illustrates a repair that completed a missing command and restored the required sequence; the archive contains the exact before/after text. Limitations and threats: (i) shared_initial_candidate semantics—our estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for a fixed initial sample, not the effect of constrained first‑pass prompting or independent multiple draws; (ii) validator coverage—deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite battery of syntactic/semantic/reachability checks and cannot detect violations outside its rule set; (iii) reduced sample size and small discordant counts—34 both‑arm infrastructure failures reduced analysed pairs to 266 and the small discordant counts limit inferential power; (iv) runtime nondeterminism—temperature is unset and no deterministic sampling seed is archived, so nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded; (v) latency H2(b) could not be evaluated because per‑episode latency was not recorded. Recommendations: future studies should (a) target task corpora with higher baseline failure rates to expose repair benefit; (b) record per‑episode latency to evaluate operational bounds; (c) expand validator coverage and include human‑in‑the‑loop escalation studies; and (d) evaluate alternative first‑pass constrained generation strategies rather than shared_initial_candidate alone.
sections.conclusion: A preregistered paired experiment (shared_initial_candidate semantics) evaluated a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) on intent→CLI tasks. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved verifier pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625). Paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle to support reanalysis and follow‑on work. References: [1] C. Wang et al., “NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?”, Proc. (2024). [2] S.Y. Long et al., “A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models,” IEEE Commun. Surveys & Tutorials, 2025. [3] R. Cadenas, “Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments,” SSRN, 2026. [4] M. Brown et al., “Lessons from the evolution of the Batfish configuration analysis tool,” SIGCOMM/Workshop (2023). [5] R. Mondal et al., “What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?”, Proc. (2023).

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (concise): Declared model used: gpt-5-mini (declared in archived execution/model_configuration.json). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Initial master prompt: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, study selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and contains no deterministic sampling seed; therefore nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded from the recorded calls. Detailed execution, artifact, and hash manifests are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration and are available for audit per the track’s reproducibility requirements.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.
Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.

H2 latency not evaluated: the preregistered H2 combined median repair iterations and median end‑to‑end latency ≤ 60 s—median repair iterations = 0 (archived provider_call_audit supports this), but per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore H2(b) could not be assessed.

External validity: tasks derive from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
